newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Ethnic Russians face grim future in rebel Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ethnic Russians face grim future in rebel Chechnya.

text.p: Raya choked back her tears and huddled closer to the small makeshift bonfire for warmth.
"If only summer would come sooner," she said. "It's so much easier living like this in the summer."
Raya and her husband Volodya are Russian pensioners caught up in the maelstrom of Chechnya.
They have been living rough amid the rubble of the Chechen capital Grozny for nearly a year since their home was flattened by Russian troops trying to crush the region's pro-independence guerrillas.

Sitting on upturned cannisters next to a snow-covered rubbish tip, their few remaining possessions packed into plastic bags at their feet, the elderly Russians make a pitiful sight. They said there were many others like them.
"We have nowhere to go. We lost everything in the war. Everything was burned, destroyed -- documents, money, everything," said Raya, a former shop assistant.

The couple sleep in burnt-out buildings or abandoned cellars. They are too proud to beg but the Chechens offer them food and old clothes and they also scrape together money by selling reusable bottles.
"Even if we had the money to go to Russia, what would we do there? Our home was here," said Volodya, a retired engineer.
GROZNY COMPLETELY RUINED AFTER BITTER WAR
Nearly five months after a peace deal halted fighting between Russian troops and the Chechen rebels, Grozny remains a complete wreck with hardly any sign of reconstruction.
In the centre of the once easy-going southern town, most buildings are little more than charred shells. Windows, doors and roofs were ripped away by months of relentless Russian shelling.
Tens of thousands of people, mostly civilians, died in the fighting. Now Russia has withdrawn its last troops from the tiny breakaway territory ahead of elections planned for January 27.

Before President Boris Yeltsin sent in troops to crush Chechnya's separatists in December 1994, about 400,000 ethnic Russians lived in Chechnya -- about a third of the total population -- but local people said very few remained.

It is one of the Chechen war's sad ironies that ethnic Russians bore the brunt of Moscow's military onslaught because, unlike most Chechens, they did not have relatives to shelter with in the mountains.
RUSSIANS WITH HOMES AFRAID TO LEAVE THEM
Even Russians who still have a roof over their heads face a bleak and uncertain future.
"I don't want to leave but I don't see how it is possible to stay. We are no longer wanted here," said Olga Kravchenko, who works for Russia's gas giant Gazprom.
"The war was not our fault. We don't like having our homes bombed either, but of course the Chechens think of us too as being somehow to blame. It's difficult."
Kravchenko's home was also destroyed by Russian bombardment. She and her 10-year-old daughter Diana live in rented accommodation but are afraid to venture out after dark.
"You hear all the time of robberies, of attacks against Russians," she said.
This month two Russian Orthodox priests were abducted after being lured out of Grozny in search of the grave of a third priest who was killed nearly a year ago.
The priests' fate remains a mystery and is another worrying sign for the mostly elderly or immobile Russians still in Chechnya.
Two Russian families in Grozny were shot dead in their homes late last year, but the Chechen authorities insisted that the killings were not politically motivated.
THEY BLAME RUSSIA, NOT CHECHENS, FOR THEIR PLIGHT

Despite fears of being robbed or even killed, the Russians have few bad things to say about their Chechen neighbours. Their anger is directed against their own army and government, which they hold responsible for the war.
"I never thought Russia would fire on its own people. Surely it is impermissible to fire on children," Kravchenko said, pulling her daughter towards her.
"The Chechen people are mostly good to us and very hospitable," she added, echoing the comments of her compatriots in Grozny. "I have no problems with them."
Her friend Lena, who works at the local power station, said Russians and Chechens had always lived happily side by side.

Asked about the forthcoming elections, both women said they would probably vote for Aslan Maskhadov, the former chief commander of the rebel guerrillas widely seen as the most pragmatic and conciliatory of the presidential candidates.

But they also expressed concern about Chechnya breaking away completely from Russia and becoming a full-fledged Islamic state. "Our customs are different. We would feel out of place here," said Kravchenko.
For now, though, mere survival is the Russians' main concern.
"I have not been paid since last February," said Yelena, referring to the problem of chronic salary arrears that afflicts many other workers across the Russian Federation.
Asked how they survived without their wages, the women said they traded things at Grozny's still-bustling bazaar.
"We survived the war and we'll survive this too," said their elderly neighbour Valya with a fatalistic Slavic shrug.
"Besides we were raised in Soviet times," added Kravchenko. "We can't get out of the habit of going to work even when they have stopped paying us."
